title: Small Intestine Anatomy
descriptor: Three Regions, Villi & Absorption, Mesentery & Blood Supply, Coeliac & Crohn's Disease
intro: The small intestine is the part of the digestive tract that runs from the pylorus of the stomach to the ileocaecal valve, where it meets the large intestine. It has three regions, the duodenum, jejunum and ileum, and it is the site of most chemical digestion and almost all absorption. Enzymes from the pancreas and from the intestinal lining do most of the chemical digestion, and bile salts help to emulsify lipids in the duodenum.

sections.heading: Location and relations
sections.body: The three regions follow one another from the stomach, with no clear dividing line between the jejunum and the ileum. The duodenum lies just below the stomach and curves around the head of the pancreas in a C shape. Its first part is intraperitoneal, whereas its second, third and fourth parts are retroperitoneal, lying behind the peritoneum. The jejunum and ileum are also intraperitoneal, and the mesentery carries their blood vessels, nerves and lymphatics. The jejunum lies mainly in the left upper quadrant of the abdomen and the ileum mainly in the right lower quadrant. The ileum ends at the ileocaecal valve, which separates it from the large intestine.

sections.heading: Regions
sections.body: The duodenum is the shortest and widest part of the small intestine, and it has four parts: the bulb, the descending part, the horizontal part and the ascending part. Bile and pancreatic secretions enter the descending part through the ampulla of Vater, where the main pancreatic duct joins the bile duct to form the hepatopancreatic ampulla that opens into the duodenum. The ileum, the final region, is the longest part of the small intestine. In life the whole small intestine is about three metres long, and in a cadaver it is about twice as long because muscle tone is lost. The regions also differ in what they absorb: the duodenum is the major site of iron absorption, while the terminal ileum absorbs vitamin B12, which needs intrinsic factor made in the stomach.

sections.heading: Wall and lining
sections.body: The wall of the small intestine has four layers: the mucosa, submucosa, muscularis propria and serosa. Deep circular folds (plicae circulares), villi and microvilli together greatly increase the surface area available for absorption. The microvilli give the mucosa a fuzzy appearance called the brush border, and the absorptive cells synthesise digestive enzymes and place them in the membranes of their microvilli. Cells that arise in the intestinal glands include absorptive cells, goblet cells, Paneth cells (which secrete lysozyme) and several types of enteroendocrine cell, and some of the hormone-secreting types occur only in the duodenum, or only in the duodenum and jejunum. Intestinal juice is a mixture of water and mucus. The epithelial cells are renewed rapidly.

sections.heading: Blood supply, nerves and lymph
sections.body: The small intestine receives arterial blood from the coeliac trunk and the superior mesenteric artery. In the duodenum, the superior pancreaticoduodenal artery supplies the upper part and the inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery the lower part. The jejunum and ileum are supplied by jejunal and ileal branches of the superior mesenteric artery, which run through the mesentery. Veins follow the arteries and drain into the superior mesenteric vein, which joins the splenic vein to form the portal vein. Lymph begins in the mucosa and drains to nodes along the mesentery, the arterial arcades and the superior mesenteric artery, and from there to the coeliac nodes. Sympathetic fibres from the superior mesenteric ganglia reach the jejunum and ileum through the superior mesenteric plexus; they reduce secretion and motility and cause vasoconstriction.

sections.heading: Function: digestion and absorption
sections.body:
In the duodenum, bile salts and pancreatic enzymes emulsify and break down lipids. Brush-border enzymes then complete the digestion of carbohydrates and proteins. Complex carbohydrates are first hydrolysed by salivary and pancreatic amylases, and only monosaccharides are absorbed by the lining cells, called enterocytes; proteins are reduced to small peptides and free amino acids.

Blood capillaries in the villi take up carbohydrates and proteins, while the lacteals take up fats. Enterocytes package fats into chylomicrons, which carry dietary fat and fat-soluble vitamins; these are too large for the basement membranes of blood capillaries, so they enter the larger pores of the lacteals. Water absorption follows osmotic gradients, helped by aquaporins in the intestinal membranes. Segmentation, in which rings of smooth muscle contract and relax, shoves chyme back and forth rather than moving it along the tract.

sections.heading: Clinical relevance
sections.body:
Coeliac disease is an autoimmune condition triggered by gluten that damages the lining of the small intestine: the finger-like villi flatten, so nutrients are absorbed less efficiently and deficiencies, iron among them, can follow. Crohn's disease is a long-term condition in which abnormal immune reactions cause inflammation in the digestive tract, most commonly in the small intestine and the beginning of the large intestine. Ulcers can form in the duodenum as well as the stomach; the NHS names H. pylori infection and regular use of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory painkillers as the main causes.

Short bowel syndrome develops when the small intestine is shortened or damaged and cannot absorb enough nutrients, most often after surgery to remove part of it. Small intestine cancers include adenocarcinoma, sarcoma, neuroendocrine tumours, gastrointestinal stromal tumours and lymphoma, and weight loss and abdominal pain can be signs, although other conditions can cause the same symptoms. Persistent symptoms should be assessed by a clinician.

sections.heading: How the small intestine is investigated
sections.body: A gastroscopy checks inside the food pipe, the stomach and the top of the intestine using a thin tube with a camera, and a small sample of cells (a biopsy) may be collected. The top of the intestine is the duodenum, the first region of the small intestine. The NHS says it can help find out what is causing digestive symptoms, and it can also be used for treatment, such as removing growths or stopping bleeding. For coeliac disease, the NHS describes two main methods of diagnosis: a blood test that looks for antibodies and a biopsy that can help confirm the diagnosis.
